newsitem.title: USA: Hong Kong ex-tobacco exec loses extradition appeal.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong ex-tobacco exec loses extradition appeal.

text.p: A former tobacco company executive, accused of accepting more than $3 million in bribes, lost his fight on Thursday against extradition to Hong Kong from the United States.

The U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a lower court ruling that barred the federal government from turning former British American Tobacco Co. executive Lui Kin-Hong over to Hong Kong authorities.

Lui's case raised a question regarding U.S.-China policy: would the United States, under an existing extradition treaty with Britain, continue to send defendants to Hong Kong for trial in a system that will soon be controlled by the People's Republic of China?
Both sides agreed that Lui would not receive a trial before July 1, when China takes over the Crown Colony from Britain.

When the chief judge of the U.S. District Court in Boston Joseph Tauro, ruled in January that the existing treaty language was never intended to apply to a totalitarian or other nondemocratic regime, the case quickly caused an uproar in Hong Kong.

But the appeals court noted Lui, now a Canadian citizen, "is wanted for economic, not political, activities whose criminality is fully recognized in the United States. His extradition is sought by the current Hong Kong regime, a colony of Great Britain, which, as Lui himself points out, is one of this country's most trusted treaty partners....There is nothing here which shocks the conscience of the court."

Furthermore the three judge panel said while the United States does not have an extradition treaty with China, it has entered into one with the new Hong Kong Special Administration Region, which Beijing said "will enjoy a high degree of autonomy except in foreign and defence affairs."
The new treaty, submitted to the U.S. Senate March 3, will not go into force until the legislators give their advice and consent.
Lui, who was arrested at Boston's Logan International Airport, when he flew from Canada to visit a sick friend in December 1995, was ordered held without bail.
The appeals panel stayed its ruling for 14 days to give Lui a chance to appeal. After that time, a certificate of extradictablity will be delivered to the U.S. State Department, the panel ruled.
